display: Mahalia Jackson was born in New Orleans on October 26, 1911, the third of six children of a man who was a longshoreman by day, a barber by night and a clergyman on Sunday. Her mother died when she was six, and she was raised by an aunt in a poor but respectable home; she left school in the eighth grade to work as a cook and washerwoman.

In 1928 she moved to Chicago, worked as a hotel maid and laundress, and joined the Greater Salem Baptist Church, where she became a soloist. She never learned to read music. After her Carnegie Hall debut on October 4, 1950, she began touring abroad in 1952, and toured widely for the rest of her life.

She was closely associated with the civil rights movement and sang at the March on Washington in 1963 before Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech. When she moved into an all-white neighborhood on the South Side of Chicago, a bullet was fired through a window of her home.

Touring the segregated South for as many as 200 dates a year, she and her company had trouble finding safe places to sleep, eat and buy gas, sometimes slept in her car, lived on bags of fruit and drove half the night, and she arrived so exhausted she was almost dizzy when she sang; she insisted on being paid in cash because checks were often refused.

Before and during her first European tour in 1952 she had difficulty breathing during and after performances and severe abdominal cramping, sang many shows in pain, lost a great deal of weight and finally cancelled the tour. On her return she had a hysterectomy, at which numerous granulomas were found in her abdomen, and she was diagnosed with sarcoidosis. From then on she had occasional bouts of fatigue and shortness of breath that became more frequent as her schedule filled.

In 1964, weeks after her marriage, she could not stop coughing on the drive home from a concert in St. Louis and admitted herself to a Chicago hospital. The diagnosis given in public was heart strain and exhaustion; her doctors told her privately that she had had a heart attack and that sarcoidosis was now in her heart. Recovery took a year, during which she could not tour or record and lost about 50 pounds; afterwards she had near-constant fatigue, bouts of tachycardia and high blood pressure. From 1964 she was in and out of hospitals, and physicians warned her of exhaustion from her itineraries.
She was hospitalized for heart trouble in the fall of 1967.
By the late 1960s she had inflammation in her eyes and painful cramps in her legs and hands; she cut short a European tour in 1968 for health reasons.
In 1971 she toured Japan, India and Europe; she became ill on tour in Germany, where she gave her last concert in Munich, and was flown home to Chicago and hospitalized in the fall.
She died on January 27, 1972, at Little Company of Mary Hospital in Evergreen Park, Illinois, at 60, after several years of poor health.

The cause of her death is recorded differently: a heart seizure (The New York Times), heart failure (PBS), a heart attack (Biography.com), heart complications at home (New Orleans Historical), and death in recovery after surgery for a bowel obstruction, which one account attributes to sarcoidosis (Wikipedia, TheWrap).

That her heart disease, and the heart trouble that recurred until her death, was cardiac sarcoidosis is a retrospective interpretation. It rests on the private account of her doctors in 1964 reported by her biographer; the public diagnoses were heart strain, exhaustion and heart trouble.

Breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough for three months, worse on tour, with tiredness and chest tightness; she can no longer hold long phrases; bilateral hilar lymph node enlargement on today's chest radiograph; granulomas were reported at an abdominal operation twelve years ago, with no pathology report available: sarcoidosis must be confirmed by tissue and other causes excluded

synthetic_reason: Synthetic lung-function goal.

synthetic_reason: Synthetic cardiac goal.

synthetic_reason: Synthetic treatment goal.

display: Back on stage with a schedule she can sustain, with her voice protected

display: Pulmonology (sarcoidosis) consultation within two weeks, with EBUS-guided lymph node sampling arranged directly from the referral, to confirm the diagnosis and plan treatment
synthetic_reason: Synthetic specialist consultation booked at intake.

display: Diagnosis of suspected sarcoidosis: chest radiograph and CT of the chest, tissue by EBUS-guided needle aspiration rather than mediastinoscopy, stains and cultures for mycobacteria and fungi, an interferon-gamma release assay and HIV test to exclude other causes; serum ACE is not used to make or exclude the diagnosis
synthetic_reason: Synthetic diagnostic plan.

display: Screening every patient with suspected sarcoidosis for other organ involvement: ECG, serum calcium with 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, creatinine, liver tests and alkaline phosphatase, complete blood count, TSH, and an eye examination; stop the calcium and vitamin D supplement while calcium is high
synthetic_reason: Synthetic screening plan.

display: Cardiac evaluation for suspected cardiac sarcoidosis (abnormal ECG and palpitations): 24-hour Holter monitoring, echocardiogram, cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement, and cardiac FDG-PET with a dietary preparation, all before glucocorticoids begin; cardiology and electrophysiology review
synthetic_reason: Synthetic cardiac plan decided at the consultation.

display: Treatment of cardiac and pulmonary sarcoidosis: prednisone 40 mg daily, tapered over about six months toward 5 to 10 mg, with methotrexate 15 mg weekly (increased to 20 mg) and folic acid, continued for at least a year for cardiac disease; repeat FDG-PET after about six months
synthetic_reason: Synthetic treatment decided when cardiac involvement was confirmed.

display: Methotrexate safety: hepatitis B and C screening before starting, blood count, liver tests and creatinine every two to four weeks for the first three months and then every eight to twelve weeks, no alcohol, and no trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole while on methotrexate
synthetic_reason: Synthetic methotrexate monitoring decided at the start of treatment.

display: Glucocorticoid protection: bone density scan and FRAX, alendronate weekly, dietary calcium only (no supplements while calcium was high), vitamin D replaced cautiously once calcium is normal, with calcium rechecked; atovaquone pneumocystis prophylaxis while prednisone is 20 mg or more with methotrexate; glucose, blood pressure, weight, mood, sleep and eye pressure checks
synthetic_reason: Synthetic protection plan decided at the start of treatment.

display: Vaccination before immunosuppression: PCV20, recombinant zoster vaccine, hepatitis B vaccine for a non-immune adult, influenza and COVID-19 vaccines; no live vaccines while on prednisone and methotrexate
synthetic_reason: Synthetic vaccination plan decided at the start of treatment.

display: Arrhythmia risk: metoprolol for ventricular ectopy; electrophysiology study for a left ventricular ejection fraction above 35 percent with scar on MRI and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, and a dual-chamber defibrillator if sustained ventricular tachycardia is induced; remote device monitoring, including on tour
synthetic_reason: Synthetic arrhythmia plan decided when cardiac involvement was confirmed.

display: Performing and travel: concerts paused until the defibrillator wound has healed and the first device check is done, then a lighter schedule with rest days, voice care, and a travel letter with her device card and medicine list; no driving for one week after the implant
synthetic_reason: Synthetic plan for her work decided with her when treatment began.
